hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to prominent, elongated linear structures—typically cylindrical rods, metallic bars, or sharp ridges—oriented diagonally from the upper-left to the lower-right. These features are characterized by a strong longitudinal specular highlight or gradient that conveys a 3D tubular form, and frequently appear as repeating parallel patterns such as screw threads, zipper teeth, or aligned bars. The neuron is invariant to the specific object identity (e.g., pencils, hardware, piano keys) and material, as long as the diagonal geometry and high contrast are maintained. The activating feature is consistently bright white, silver, or light grey, set against a low-key background of black, dark charcoal, or deep grey, creating a stark light-on-dark polarity. Spatially, the linear element typically traverses the center of the frame, spanning 60–90% of the image diagonal while occupying roughly 10–30% of the image width.
